Printing a message together with its answer lets the reader watch a piece of business open and close. giraldus-cambrensis-topography-of-irelan:

boas-central-eskimo-1888:

rhys-celtic-heathendom-1888:

toussenel-les-juifs-rois-de-l-epoque-188:

Three people, one set, and talk as a weapon: the design is flawless and pitiless in execution here. Directors rank it with Miss Julie as Strindberg's most actable and most revived one-act work.
storm-rider-white-horse-1888:
Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse in 1888, a German novella set on the Frisian coast. Hauke Haien is a bright farm boy who rises to become dike master. He dreams of a new, safer dike against the North Sea. Villagers mock his plans and fear his pride and ambition.

Storm frames the tale as a story told on a stormy night, with hints of a ghostly rider. Hauke's new dike is tested by a great flood. Family loss and local distrust deepen the gloom. The novella blends realism with legend and dread. It is Storm's last and most famous work, a classic of German fiction.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-4-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 4 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Attention turns east to Justinian and the Byzantine Empire. Belisarius, Justinian's great general, reconquers parts of Italy and Africa from the Goths and Vandals. Law receives its classic code under Justinian's direction.

The plague that struck the empire in the 540s gets a chilling account. Gibbon also surveys Persia and the early state of Arabia before Muhammad. His irony spares neither monks nor emperors. The volume shows the History's true scope: a whole civilization's world. Readers admire its learning on law, war, and faith alike.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-5-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 5 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Muhammad and the Arab conquests enter the narrative in this volume. Gibbon gives a long account of Arabia, the Prophet's life, and the Koran. Arab armies then sweep Persia, Syria, Egypt, and Spain with stunning speed.

Later chapters treat the iconoclast emperors, the Bulgarians, and the state of the Eastern Empire. Gibbon's treatment of Islam was unusually fair for his age. His irony returns in full for monks and relic cults. The volume carries the story to the eve of the Crusades. Its breadth shows why the History is called a world in itself.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-6-1788:
Edward Gibbon completed his Decline and Fall with Volume 6 in 1788. The final volume covers the Crusades, the Mongols, and the last centuries of Byzantium. It ends with the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. Gibbon closes by surveying the ruins of Rome itself.

His last pages reflect on the whole arc from empire's height to ruin. The siege of 1453 is told with grim grandeur. Gibbon finished the work in Lausanne and recalled sitting in the Capitol as a young man when the idea first struck him. The six volumes form the greatest history ever written in English, by wide consent.
white-great-controversy-1888:
Ellen White, co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, published The Great Controversy Between Christ and Satan in 1888. The book tells a sweeping story of cosmic conflict, from the fall of Lucifer to the promised new earth. Adventists treat it as the movement's central prophetic history.

White follows the fight through the fall of Jerusalem, the early church, the Reformation, and the last days still to come. Each age, in her telling, turns on whether God's law and Sabbath are honored or set aside. The narrative gave her church a story of itself that still shapes Adventist reading of world events.
molinos-spiritual-guide-1688:
Miguel de Molinos was a Spanish priest in Rome whose Spiritual Guide, Englished in 1688, taught the quiet way of prayer to eager readers. The book won praise across Europe and, for a time, papal approval in high places. Then Rome condemned its propositions, and Molinos died in prison.

Molinos tells the soul to lay aside effort, images, and even anxious self-examination, resting in God without grasping. Critics charged that such quiet kills moral effort and the church's sacraments alike. His fall shaped European mysticism by warning it where the line of suspicion lay. Its short chapters made it a handbook readers could carry and reread.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol1-1888:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky published Volume 1 of The Secret Doctrine in 1888, with the subtitle Cosmogenesis. Blavatsky, a cofounder of the Theosophical Society, claimed the book rested on an ancient hidden text, the Stanzas of Dzyan. Volume 1 treats the birth and order of the universe.

Blavatsky described worlds forming in great cycles, guided by spiritual beings, long before human life appears. She set Hindu, Buddhist, and other teachings beside the science of her day and claimed they agreed. Critics attacked her sources, but readers flocked to the system. The volume became the founding text of modern Theosophy and shaped occult thought far beyond her society.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol2-1888:
Volume 2 of Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine, Anthropogenesis, also appeared in 1888. Where Volume 1 treated the cosmos, Volume 2 treated humankind. Blavatsky again built on the Stanzas of Dzyan, which she said held a secret record of human origins.

She described root races, early human forms said to arise on lost lands such as Lemuria and Atlantis. Apes, in her account, came from humans rather than the other way round, a direct clash with Darwin. She mixed myth, geology, and scripture into one vast scheme. The volume completed the work that made Theosophy a world movement and fed later lost-race and ancient-astronaut lore.
proudhon-system-economical-contradiction:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Proudhon's System of Economical Contradictions in 1888. Proudhon had issued the work in 1846 with the subtitle The Philosophy of Misery. Tucker, Proudhon's chief American champion, spread his books through his journal Liberty and its press.

Proudhon marched through the ideas of political economy, division of labor, machinery, competition, and monopoly, finding each both good and harmful. That method of paired contradictions drove Karl Marx to answer with The Poverty of Philosophy, a famous attack. The quarrel split the young socialist movement. Tucker's translation lets English readers judge Proudhon's dense, daring critique of political economy in the form that provoked Marx.
hutton-theory-of-earth-1788:
James Hutton presented his Theory of the Earth paper in 1788 to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, in its Transactions. Hutton, a Scottish farmer and naturalist, argued that the Earth's features are the work of slow forces still at work today. That claim opened the door to deep time.

Rocks, Hutton said, are worn down, laid down in seas, hardened, lifted, and worn again in an endless cycle. At sites such as Siccar Point, tilted layers under flat ones proved to him a past far longer than the received chronology allowed. His famous line found no vestige of a beginning. The paper is the founding document of modern geology.
kipling-plain-tales-1888:
Rudyard Kipling was a teenage newspaper reporter in India when he wrote these stories. Plain Tales from the Hills, published in 1888, was his first book for a wide audience. He wrote it at Simla, the summer capital where British officials escaped the heat.

The forty short tales show Anglo-Indian society in miniature: flirtations, feuds, pranks, and sudden tragedies. Young officers and clever widows scheme through the season while disease and distance shadow everything. Kipling's style is quick, dry, and knowing far beyond his years. The book announced a major storyteller and remains a sharp picture of the British Raj at play.
morris-dream-john-ball-1888:
William Morris, the designer and poet, had become a committed socialist by the 1880s. He published A Dream of John Ball in 1888, pairing it with a shorter prose piece, A King's Lesson. The dream tale first ran in a socialist newspaper, Commonweal, which Morris helped run.

A modern socialist narrator dreams himself back to 1381, during the Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler. He talks through the night with John Ball, the rebel priest who preached that things would never be well while some were masters and others servants. Morris uses the rising to ask what his own movement must learn. The book blends history, hope, and warning.
stevenson-black-arrow-1888:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote The Black Arrow as a serial for a boys' magazine, using a pen name. It appeared in book form in 1888, after Treasure Island had made him famous. Stevenson himself thought it rather careless work, but young readers loved it.

During the Wars of the Roses, young Dick Shelton finds his father was murdered by his own guardian. He joins the outlaws of Tunstall Forest, who sign their revenge with black arrows. Battles, escapes, and a rescue-romance follow as Dick shifts sides in England's civil war. Richard of Gloucester, the future Richard III, appears as a chilling young fighter. The novel is a fast, rousing adventure of the fifteenth century.
schiller-revolt-of-the-netherlands-1788:
Schiller turned from plays to history with his History of the Revolt of the Netherlands, published in 1788. Edward Backhouse Eastwick translated the work into English in the nineteenth century. The book tells how the Dutch provinces rose against Spanish rule in the 1500s.

Schiller traces the clash of faith, taxes, and foreign rule that drove the revolt. William of Orange and the Duke of Alva stand out as the great opposed figures. The narrative gave Schiller the ground from which Don Carlos had grown. It also won him respect as a historian, not only a playwright. Readers still value its clear story of a small people's fight for its liberties.
queiros-os-maias-1888:
Eça de Queirós published Os Maias in Portugal in 1888, and the text here is the Portuguese original. Carlos da Maia, last hope of a great Lisbon family, is raised by his grandfather Afonso after family tragedy. Carlos studies medicine, idles in high society, and falls in love with a married stranger, Maria Eduarda.

A buried secret about Maria's birth turns love into horror for them both. Around the pair, Eça paints Lisbon's politics, salons, and newspapers with amused disgust. The novel tracks the Maia family's slow decline across three generations. Portuguese readers rank Os Maias as their greatest novel. Its English translation of 1925 exists but could not be staged here.
walker-reincarnation-forgotten-truth-188:
E. D. Walker published Reincarnation: A Study of Forgotten Truth at Boston in 1888, with Houghton Mifflin. Walker wrote the first systematic English survey of reincarnation beliefs across the world's religions. Hindu, Buddhist, Greek, early Christian, and modern witnesses file through his chapters in turn.

He gathers Plato, the Upanishads, Origen, and the theosophists of his own day into one argument. The book introduced the doctrine to the late nineteenth-century English-reading public at large. For decades it stood as the standard reference on the subject in English. Walker writes as an advocate, yet his learning is broad and his sources are named. The survey still serves readers tracing the idea's long, wandering history.
zosimos-panopolis-oeuvres-berthelot-1888:
Zosimos of Panopolis, an Egyptian Greek who wrote around 300 CE, is the earliest alchemist whose name and works survive. Marcellin Berthelot and C. E. Ruelle printed his works in their great edition of Greek alchemy in 1888. The text here gives Zosimos in the editors' French translation.

Zosimos writes letters to a woman pupil, Theosebeia, full of visions, furnaces, and coded talk of metals turning toward gold. He quotes older masters and dreams of a divine water that frees the spirit from the body. His pages are the fountainhead of the alchemical art in the West. Every later adept, Greek, Arab, and Latin, drew from this spring.
pseudo-democritus-physica-mystica-berthe:
The Physica et Mystica, questions on nature and secret things, claims the name of Democritus, the laughing philosopher of atoms. In fact it comes from Bolos of Mendes, writing in Egypt in the first or second century. It is the oldest layer of Greek alchemy. Berthelot and Ruelle printed it in 1888, in French translation.

Recipes for making gold, silver, purple dye, and gems fill the book, mixed with spells and the lore of like acting on like. A letter to Leucippe travels with the text. The work shows alchemy at its birth, half craft and half mystery. All the later art, Greek and Arab, grows from these pages.
synesius-alchemist-commentary-berthelot-:
An alchemist named Synesius, not the famous bishop, wrote this commentary on the book ascribed to Democritus. He casts his teaching as a dialogue with Dioscorus, a priest of Alexandria. Berthelot and Ruelle printed the text in 1888 in their edition of the Greek alchemists, in French translation.

Synesius unpacks the riddles of the master: what the divine water is, how metals are born from mercury and sulfur, and why the art hides in code. His commentary became the standard teaching text of the Greek school. Students of alchemy read Democritus through Synesius for centuries. The little dialogue is a key that still fits the oldest locks of the art.
olympiodorus-alchemist-art-sacre-berthel:
Olympiodorus of Thebes, a scholar of the sixth century, wrote a long commentary on Zosimos and on the sayings of the old alchemists. His work On the Sacred Art is given here in the French version of Berthelot and Ruelle, from their 1888 edition of the Greek alchemists. Olympiodorus read the art through Neoplatonic thought.

He treats the metals, the egg of the philosophers, and the work of turning base stuff toward gold as signs of a deeper order. His pages carried the alchemy of Alexandria into the Byzantine world. Without such bridges, the Greek art would not have reached the Arabs or the Latin West. The commentary is dense, learned, and strange.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-3-1888:
Henry Charles Lea closed his History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages with this third volume in 1888. It turns from the map of the tribunal to special subjects that cross all lands. Lea's calm, record-based method made the set the standard work in English.

The Knights Templar and their fall, the trial of Joan of Arc, and the crimes of Gilles de Rais fill the great case studies. Lea then anatomizes the Inquisition itself: its books, its prisons, its money, and its men. He ends with the intellectual price the system charged the church. The three volumes together remain the base on which all later study builds.
dellon-history-of-the-inquisition-at-goa:
Charles Dellon, a French doctor, fell into the hands of the Inquisition at Goa and lived to write the tale. His Relation de l'Inquisition de Goa appeared in French in 1687, and this English version followed in 1688. Dellon had spent his youth traveling in India when the Holy Office seized him in 1673.

He tells of the secret arrest, the cells, and the long silence. The charges against him were never shown. At last he walked in the auto-da-fé of 1676 in the procession of the condemned. His book carried the horror of Goa across Protestant Europe. It fixed the Inquisition's image in the English mind for two centuries. Few eyewitness tales of the tribunal match it.
geheime-figuren-rosenkreuzer-1785-1788:
Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer, printed at Altona from 1785 to 1788, is the emblem book of the Gold- und Rosenkreuzer order. The German title means the secret figures of the Rosicrucians, drawn from the 1500s and 1600s. The order that issued it was the leading Rosicrucian body of its century.

Sixteen engraved plates carry the book, each plate a dense symbolic image. Around the plates runs the order's own commentary, steeped in alchemy and theosophy, two paths to hidden knowledge of God and nature. The volume became the order's most famous printed work. Its plates still shape how the Rose Cross is pictured today.
monluc-commentaries-cotton-1688:
Blaise de Monluc, a Gascon soldier, wrote his Commentaires in 1592 about the wars he fought under King Henri II of France. Charles Cotton's English translation, first made in 1674, appears here in the printing of 1688. Monluc rose from common soldier to marshal by wounds, daring, and a fierce will to be remembered.

His memoir is all camp and battlefield: sieges, charges, feuds, and the raw talk of men at war. King Henry IV is said to have called the book the soldier's breviary, the handbook every fighter should keep. Monluc spares no one, least of all himself, in telling how war really felt. The Commentaries remain a classic soldier's memoir of the 1500s.
reid-essays-active-powers-1788:
Reid's Essays on the Active Powers of Man, from 1788, turn Thomas Reid from the mind's knowing to its doing. Five essays, complete here, treat the powers that move a person to act. Will stands first, then the springs of action: appetite, desire, and affection, summed up as motives.

Morals close the work, as Reid grounds right and wrong in a moral sense open to reason. The book is his moral philosophy entire, the partner of his Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Against theories that made humans mere bundles of feeling, Reid defends free, rational agency. His calm system shaped moral teaching in Scotland and America for a century.
bosanquet-logic-vol1-1888:
Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, from 1888, opens with volume one here. Morphology is the study of forms, and Bosanquet studies the forms of thought itself: how judgment and inference grow, stage by stage. He wrote as a British idealist, in the wake of Hegel, against the dry formal logic of the schools.

For Bosanquet, a judgment is not a label pasted on the world but the mind building its world into a system. Inference, likewise, is the self-development of knowledge toward a coherent whole. Volume one lays that living account of thought from its roots upward. The work remains a summit of idealist logic, exacting and rich.
bosanquet-logic-vol2-1888:
Volume two completes Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, of 1888. Bosanquet, the British idealist, treats logic not as a rule book for arguments but as the anatomy of knowledge in growth. The two volumes together form his fullest statement on how thought builds a world.

The second volume carries the account of judgment and inference toward the system that all knowledge seeks. Each form of thought, for Bosanquet, corrects the one before it and points beyond itself. Truth lives in the coherence of the finished whole, not in single, severed claims. Readers who finish the Logic hold the British idealist theory of knowledge at its most developed.
bellamy-looking-backward-1888:
Edward Bellamy imagined the year 2000 in Looking Backward, published in 1888. His hero, Julian West, sleeps in 1887 Boston and wakes in the Boston of 2000. That future city runs on socialist lines he could not have dreamed. A guide explains the new order of work, pay, and goods.

An industrial army organizes labor, and equal credit replaces wages and cash. Shops, music, and meals all run as public services in his design. The novel sold hugely and launched clubs devoted to its program. It became the era's best known utopian classic. Readers still visit its future to test their own hopes. The frame tale stays charming.
davenport-death-blow-spiritualism-1888:
Margaret Fox Kane confessed her fraud to reporter Reuben Briggs Davenport, and his 1888 book told the world. The Fox sisters' rappings of 1848 had launched modern spiritualism. Kane, one of the sisters, now described how the knocks were made. Davenport, of the New York World, shaped her confession into The Death-Blow to Spiritualism.

The book gives the true story of the sisters, in her account, trick by trick. Toe joints, she said, made the famous rapping sounds. Believers fought the confession, and Kane later withdrew it. Historians still treat the volume as a key insider record. It broke the founding story of spiritualism open.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol8-1888:
Eight years separated Volume VIII of the Guiding Symptoms from the first, and it arrived in 1888. The delay shows in the care of the editing, as Hering's students worked through boxes of proving notes. Remedies still march in alphabetical order, their symptoms filed under body regions.

Few books in the school carry this much raw clinical memory. A prescriber chasing an odd, precise symptom, the kind that names one remedy alone, would search here first. The marks of rank beside each line keep the search short. Volume VIII keeps the promise of the title: guidance, not mere bulk.
hopkins-scientific-christian-mental-prac:
Emma Curtis Hopkins earned the name teacher of teachers, and Scientific Christian Mental Practice, from 1888, is her textbook. Hopkins trained Charles Fillmore and a generation of New Thought ministers in her Chicago classrooms. Her course builds from a Statement of Being through denials and affirmations, step by ordered step.

Students learn to deny error's power and affirm the good they claim as real. The method is mental, yet Hopkins gives it the shape of a strict spiritual discipline. Her book systematized New Thought teaching, and its structure shaped the movement's churches and classes for decades.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
Volume Two of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography came out in 1888, running from Crane to Grimshaw. Editors Wilson and Fiske kept the pace of a life for nearly every notable name. The set was sold by subscription across the country.

This volume's span covers many founders, Civil War officers, and men of letters of the young republic. Each entry gives birth, career, works, and death in tight, factual prose. Steel portraits mark the most famous names. Read across the six volumes, Appletons' forms a portrait gallery of the nation as the Victorian age wished to remember it.

Volume Three of Appletons' Cyclopaedia, also from 1888, continues the alphabet from Grinnell to Lockwood. Wilson and Fiske's dictionary was halfway done, with thousands of American lives already in print. The work's scale was unmatched in its day.

Governors, judges, explorers, and divines fill these pages, each weighed in a column or two. The editors include Canadians and Latin Americans whose lives touched the United States. Family details and lists of writings make the entries useful for tracing kin and careers. The volume carries the national biography through the middle letters with steady, encyclopedic calm. The print is dense, but the facts are laid out in a steady, clear order.

Volume Four of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography appeared in 1888, covering Lodge to Pickens. The dictionary had become a fixture in American libraries. Wilson and Fiske drew on family papers and earlier collections for their facts.

This stretch of the alphabet holds many Revolutionary officers, senators, and college presidents. Entries balance public deeds with private character sketches drawn from obituaries and memoirs. A few lives were polished by the families themselves, a flaw later readers learned to discount. Even so, the volume preserves facts about hundreds of figures that survive nowhere else in print. Many entries rest on obituaries clipped from the newspapers of the day.

Volume Five of Appletons' Cyclopaedia came out in 1888, running from Pickering to Sumter. The set was nearing its end, and the editors' net had caught most of the nation's notable dead and living. Subscribers received the volumes year by year.

Revolutionary statesmen, Civil War generals, and leading clergy crowd this part of the alphabet. The entries keep the house style: dates, posts, battles, books, and a closing judgment. Charles Sumter's contemporaries and Charles Sumner both appear in these pages. For students of nineteenth-century America, the volume is a dense quarry of names, dates, and careers.
plos-pone-0003388:
Chiara Begliomini and co-authors scanned human brains during grip tasks in this 2008 study. Grasping turns what the eyes see into precise hand movements. In monkeys, a known brain circuit handles that change. The team asked how the human version of the circuit behaves.

People grasped objects with the left hand or the right hand during scans. Brain activity shifted with the hand used and with the person's own handedness. Right-handed and left-handed people did not use the circuit in the same way. The study shows that hand choice shapes motor planning deep in the brain.
plos-pone-0003488:
Gita Ramjee and co-authors ran a trial of added STI protection for women in this 2008 paper. The test group used a diaphragm plus lubricant gel, with condoms. The control group used condoms alone. All women in the trial faced risk of HIV and other infections.

The trial tracked new cases of chlamydia and gonorrhea. Those are common sexually transmitted infections of the cervix. Results showed whether the added barrier gave extra protection. Such evidence guides prevention advice for women who cannot rely on condoms alone. Many women cannot count on partners to use condoms every time.
plos-pone-0003588:
A. Puppo and co-authors disturbed the egg cell's outer skeleton in this 2008 study. As eggs mature for fertilization, their inner calcium stores reorganize. That change yields a more efficient calcium response at fertilization. The actin cytoskeleton also remodels during maturation and fertilization.

Altering the cortical actin deregulated calcium signaling in the eggs. It also disrupted single-sperm fertilization and sperm entry. The skeleton is thus no passive frame but an active director. Its state helps decide whether fertilization proceeds normally. Egg quality sets the odds for in vitro fertilization in clinics worldwide. Calcium waves are one of the first signs doctors and lab staff watch for after sperm meets egg in the dish.
plos-pone-0003688:
Nyambayar Dashtsoodol, Hiroshi Watarai, Sakura Sakata, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Natural killer T cells are unusual immune cells that grow in the thymus. They were thought to come only from cells carrying both the CD4 and CD8 markers. The earliest steps of their growth stayed unclear.

The team identified precursor cells that carry neither marker, a double-negative stage. These precursors can develop into natural killer T cells as well. The extra path widens the known family tree of cells that bridge the body's fast and slow immune defenses.
plos-pone-0003788:
Annette Schneider, Dimitry Spitkovsky, Peter Riess, and colleagues published this stem cell methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many stem cell lines must first grow alongside feeder cells to stay undifferentiated and potent. Later, those feeder cells count as contamination and must be removed. The team built a way to sort the two apart.

Their technology frees stem cells from feeder cells cleanly. As the title's fairy tale puts it: the good into the pot, the bad into the crop. Pure stem cells make later experiments and therapies safer and easier to interpret.
plos-pone-0003888:
Jennifer Waldo and Michael Scherrer described a small protein from dividing yeast cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Dad1p, part of the Dam1-DASH complex. That complex sits in the kinetochore, the structure linking chromosomes to the spindle. Good links let cells split their chromosomes evenly between daughter cells.

The authors produced Dad1p in the lab and gave its first detailed description. Early data on a single part helps map how the whole complex grips chromosomes. Faults in such parts can lead to cells with the wrong chromosome count. The work supports wider studies of cell division in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
plos-pone-0003988:
Thore Egeland and Antonio Salas addressed gaps in DNA haplotype databases in 2008. Forensic and disease studies often use haploid DNA, like mitochondrial DNA. Databases of normal size hold only a fraction of all haplotypes. Users still need reliable estimates for the missing types.

Their PLOS ONE article gives methods to estimate haplotype frequency and coverage. Coverage tells how much of a population a database captures. Better estimates strengthen forensic match statistics and population studies. The work helps labs state honestly what their databases miss. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004088:
Qing Chang, Wenxue Tang, Shoeb Ahmad, and co-authors studied ear gap junctions in mice in 2008. Connexin26 and connexin30 build gap junctions in the cochlea. Mutations in either are the top cause of inherited early deafness. How their loss damages hearing was not fully clear.

Their PLOS ONE article reports metabolite transfer fails without connexin30. Gap junctions pass small molecules between cochlear cells. Mice lacking connexin30 showed that transfer compromised. The finding links a hearing protein to the ear's chemical housekeeping. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004188:
Jennifer Serwanga and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some people infected with HIV stay free of symptoms for long periods without any antiretroviral therapy. Viral control, CD4 cell loss, and HIV-specific immune responses all help decide how fast the disease moves.

The team studied therapy-naive Ugandans and their HLA-B genes, which shape which virus pieces the immune system attacks. They report that T-cell recognition of the viral Gag protein across several virus clades, tied to certain HLA-B types, correlates with slow disease progression. The link points to the kind of immune response a vaccine would want to copy.
plos-pone-0004288:
Fatemeh Malekzadeh and colleagues published this pilot study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The environmental risk factors behind Crohn's disease, a chronic inflammation of the gut, remain largely unknown. A recent suggestion blamed refrigerated food, on the theory that cold-loving bacteria could be involved.

The team ran a pilot case-control study exploring the link between Crohn's disease and early exposure to domestic refrigeration. Comparing patients' early home environments with those of controls tests whether the fridge hypothesis deserves a larger study. Unusual hypotheses need small, careful tests before big ones. The study was a pilot, meant to guide a bigger one.
plos-pone-0004388:
Radiation can cause tumors, including cancers of the colon. Yet inherited traits change how strong that effect is. Eiram Elahi, Nirosha Suraweera, Emmanouil Volikos, and co-authors hunted those traits in mice. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used Apc Min mice, a strain prone to gut growths called adenomas. They crossed that line with BALB/c mice, known to be unusually sensitive to radiation tumors.

The team counted adenomas after radiation in the crossed mice. They then mapped the DNA regions tied to higher counts. Five regions, called quantitative trait loci, controlled the outcome. Each locus is a stretch of DNA that shifts the trait. Finding them helps separate inherited risk from radiation dose itself.
plos-pone-0004488: In 2009, Perera, Tang, and Herbstman linked smog to gene switches. DNA methylation of ACSL3 tracked transplacental exposure to airborne pollutants. The NYC cohort's asthma link was probed. The neat finding connects pollution to epigenetics. The children numbered in the hundreds.
plos-pone-0004588: In 2009, Al-Zeer, Al-Younes, and Braun found an immune protein eating germs. IFN-γ-inducible Irga6 mediated host resistance to Chlamydia via autophagy. The protein triggered self-eating of the invader. The finding maps innate immunity tactics. The key defense is central.
plos-pone-0004688: In 2009, Peterson, Hare, and Iyer found big genomes easing the hunt for hidden gene switches anew. Big genomes made conserved DNA patterns stand out. The conserved patterns stood out quite clearly. The method aids genomics research today. The hunt challenge is significant.
plos-pone-0004788: In 2009, a team found blood-type genes muted by tagging anew here. ABO gene tagging killed ABO output in blood cancers anew. The blood tags vanished entirely here. The study maps cancer gene wiring well. The case share is big indeed.
zola-dream-1888:
Eliza Chase translated The Dream, Zola's novel of 1888, from the French Le Reve. Chapter one sets a hard winter in 1860, when the river Oise froze over. Snow buried the small city of Beaumont in Lower Picardy that Christmas.

A girl of nine shelters all night under the arch of Saint Agnes portal. Thin dress, torn silk kerchief, and huge shoes mark her as a lost foundling. Lacemakers in the cathedral town raise her, and she dreams of a prince. Love for a noble son brings the dream near truth. Yet dreams in Zola seldom survive daylight, and heartbreak follows in its purest kind.
lempriere-classical-dictionary-1788:
John Lemprière published his Bibliotheca Classica in 1788, a dictionary of the Greek and Roman world. Lemprière was a schoolmaster and clergyman who wanted classical learning within reach of readers without Latin and Greek. The book is better known by its short name, Lemprière's Classical Dictionary.

Thousands of entries explain gods, heroes, places, and stories from ancient myth and history. The dictionary gave poets a ready store of classical material: Keats, Byron, and Shelley all drew on it for their verse. For about a century it was the English reader's standard gateway to antiquity. Later classical dictionaries replaced it in schools, but its entries still show what educated readers of the Romantic age knew and loved.
maine-international-law-1888:
Henry Sumner Maine's International Law was published in 1888 from his Cambridge lectures of 1887. Maine, the author of Ancient Law, was the great master of the historical method in legal study. In these late lectures he turned that method on the law between nations.

Maine traces how states slowly learned to live under rules: the growth of diplomacy, the laws of war, and the treatment of neutral nations. He treats international law as a real growth from custom and treaty rather than a code handed down at once. His skepticism about grand schemes keeps the lectures grounded in practice. They were his last lectures, printed after his death in 1888. The book shows the Victorian jurist viewing world order through history's lens, and it still rewards readers who doubt easy theories of global law.
brazilian-constitution-1988:
Brazil promulgated its present constitution in October 1988, closing twenty-one years of military rule. A freely elected constituent assembly wrote the text in public, hearing thousands of popular amendments from citizens' groups. Brazilians call it the citizens' constitution, a name its makers prized.

The charter restores democracy in full: direct elections, free parties, and a free press after decades of censorship. Its bill of rights is lavish in the modern Latin American style, promising health, education, and social security as duties of the state. Workers gain detailed protections, and the environment receives its own chapter. Critics call the text unwieldy; defenders answer that its promises were the point. The law of freedom regained still governs the giant of South America, the founding act of Brazil's New Republic.

The second letter rounds out a dense month in the fullest correspondence of the 1861 record. The double report closes a month in which the London file grew by a third. A third more paper in one month shows the post at full wartime stretch.
frus-1861-d188:
On 29 April 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Mr. King as part of his first great round of orders. The letter is document 188 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The record heading gives King no post, so the letter stands on its date and its writer. April 1861 was the month Seward stocked the whole service with fresh orders. His note to King joins the first great round of direction that followed the fall of Sumter. April rounds like this one show the service being manned for war at full speed. Full speed in April set a pace the service kept through the whole year.
frus-1861-d288:
Mr. Morgan reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 6 April 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 288 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the month the Civil War began, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d88:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 27 June 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 88 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d188:
The fourth Seward letter of 10 November 1862 closes the set as Document 188 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like the other three, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London.

A four-letter mail shows how much business one legation could carry: talks with ministers, shipyard reports, press reaction, and cases of detained ships or men. No one letter tells that whole story. Preserved together, the set lets readers see the London post's full load in a single week of November 1862. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d288:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 20 June 1862, and the first is Document 288 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote a week before Lee's counterstroke drove McClellan from Richmond, at the last moment of the spring's optimism. His instructions in this pair carried the Department's line into a summer that would test it hard. Reading them now, with the sequel known, shows how much wartime policy was written in honest uncertainty. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d388:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg on 13 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 388 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-August 1862 brought the opening of the campaign that ended at Bull Run, though no one could know its result when Seward wrote. His letters to Russia that summer carried the Union's case to its friendliest hearing in Europe. This dispatch shows the Department cultivating that friendship deliberately, even while its attention was consumed by Britain and France. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d488:
On 15 March 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 488 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-March found Union forces advancing on several fronts, and Seward's letters abroad pressed the theme that the rebellion was losing ground. At The Hague the practical questions were maritime: Dutch ports, Dutch colonies, and the rules belligerent ships must obey. Pike's value to Washington lay in his blunt, newsman's grasp of Dutch opinion. An instruction like this one set the points he was to make. It even set the order he was to make them in. He would use them at his next meeting with Dutch officials.
frus-1862-d588:
On 28 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Thomas Corwin, the American minister in Mexico. The instruction is Document 588 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By late May the French were advancing into Mexico's interior and the question for Washington was how far protest could safely go. Seward's orders to Corwin kept the American position clear. The United States wished Mexico well. It opposed the European enterprise. It would not be drawn into a second war. Corwin's own instincts ran hotter, which made exact instructions necessary. The dispatch shows the leash and the trust between a secretary and a distinguished minister in the hemisphere's hardest post.
frus-1862-d688: A Mr. De Long dated this dispatch 27 February 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 688 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, one week after his letter printed just before it. The record gives his name and date but not his post or its place.
frus-1863p1-d88:
Charles Francis Adams closed his mail day with this third dispatch of 19 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 88 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three sheets in a day was no rare thing at the London post in 1863. The work spanned talks with Lord Russell, the temper of Parliament, and word on ships built for the South. This letter ends the day's set. Filed with the rest, it is part of the great run that makes this volume the chief printed source. That source tells the Union's fight to keep Britain neutral.
frus-1863p1-d188: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 7 May 1863. It is document 188 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d288:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 9 September 1863. The letter is document 288 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d388:
Washington's business with Britain on 10 February 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 388 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d488:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 2 May 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d588:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed a formal note to Secretary William H. Seward on 16 July 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d688:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 11 November 1863. It appears as document 688 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, the State Department's printed record of its wartime mail.

The day after his 10 November notes, Seward wrote again, which shows how fast matters could move. Union and British officials clashed at times over seized ships and Southern agents in British ports. Short notes like this one kept those clashes from growing. The reader gets a close look at the craft of calm words. Each line was meant to hold a line without giving offense.
plos-pbio-0020288:
Steven D. Mason, Richard A. Howlett, Matthew J. Keske, and their team tested a muscle oxygen sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. HIF-1α is a protein that reacts when oxygen runs low. The team removed it from mouse skeletal muscle and checked how the mice handled exercise.

Endurance changed when the sensor was missing, showing it helps set how muscle copes with hard work. Muscles must match blood flow and fuel use to demand, and oxygen sensing is part of that match. The study helps explain why training and altitude have the effects they do. It also warns that drugs targeting HIF pathways, now in wide study, will have real effects on exercise capacity.
plos-pone-0000088:
Yi Xing, Karen Kapur, and Wing Hung Wong addressed a data problem in gene chips in PLOS ONE in 2006. Affymetrix exon arrays measure gene activity piece by piece, exon by exon, using many small probes. Picking which probes to trust, and how to sum them into one score, decides whether the results mean anything.

The authors set out rules for probe selection and a method for computing the expression index. Faulty probes, which react to the wrong target, are a known trap in chip data. Cleaner inputs give cleaner biology. Methods papers like this one rarely make headlines, yet thousands of later studies stand on them. The exon arrays opened a window on splicing that careful math had to keep clear.
plos-pone-0000188:
Xuhua Xia published this molecular evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Protein production starts when a ribosome lands at a start signal, and the Kozak consensus sequence around that signal was thought to fine-tune the start. The author tests the +4G site in that sequence and reports it is not related to how efficiently translation begins.

A claimed rule of translation falls under direct testing here. Negative results of this sort clean up the textbook picture of how genes are read. The paper matters for anyone designing gene sequences or predicting protein output from DNA, tasks where a false rule leads to false expectations.
plos-pone-0000288:
Vanina Vergoz, Edith Roussel, Jean-Christophe Sandoz, and colleagues published this bee learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honeybees can be trained by smell using the sting extension reflex. In that reflex, a bee that senses a threat paired with an odor extends its sting. The authors reveal aversive learning in honeybees through this conditioning setup.

Bees were famous for learning rewards, learning which smells mean food. Showing they also learn aversively, which smells mean danger, completes the picture of their learning. The work gives bee neuroscience a second conditioning tool, useful for studying memory and its chemistry.
plos-pone-0000388:
Harish Babu and colleagues refined a way to grow brain precursor cells from adult mice, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their source was the dentate gyrus, one of the few brain regions that keeps making new neurons in adulthood. They cut out the tiny region and grew its precursor cells as a clean, enriched layer in culture.

The cultured cells went on to produce working granule cell-like neurons, the main cell type of the dentate gyrus. A reliable culture system like this gives researchers a steady supply of adult-born neurons to study. That helps work on how the adult brain adds new cells, and what those cells do for learning and memory.
plos-pone-0000488:
Adrian B. Hehl and colleagues tested a cell-death protein in an unusual host, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Giardia lamblia is a primitive intestinal parasite that lacks mitochondria, the cell's power stations. Bax is a protein that normally triggers cell death by acting on mitochondria. The team studied Bax function in the absence of mitochondria in this protozoan.

If Bax still works in a cell with no mitochondria, its killing mechanism must reach beyond them. Odd organisms make good tests for claims about how basic machinery works, because they strip away the usual context. The study probes how ancient and how flexible the cell-death program is.
plos-pone-0000588:
Georgia Panagiotakos and colleagues measured radiation's long shadow over brain stem cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Radiation therapy saves lives but can harm the developing or adult brain. The team studied the long-term impact of radiation on two cell pools in the brain. One pool holds stem cells. The other holds oligodendrocyte precursors, the cells that renew tissue and make myelin, the insulation of nerve fibers.

If precursor pools are depleted for good, later cognitive and repair problems have a cellular explanation. Long-term studies matter because patients, especially children, live decades after treatment. Findings like these inform how radiation doses are planned to spare the brain's regenerative reserves.
plos-pone-0000688:
Erin K. Hanson and Jack Ballantyne built a sharper DNA typing system for forensic work, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Forensic labs use Y chromosome short tandem repeats, markers called Y-STRs, to identify a male DNA donor. The method shines when male DNA hides in excess female DNA, as in many sexual assault investigations.

Commercial typing kits already existed, but each added marker raises the power to tell men apart. Their title promises ultra-high discrimination from one multiplex system, testing many markers at once. Better discrimination means fewer ambiguous matches in casework. For courts and labs, a stronger Y-STR panel is a practical advance, not just a technical one.
plos-pone-0000788:
Ricardo Núñez Miguel, Joyce Wong, Julian F. Westoll and colleagues modeled the working end of an immune alarm receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptor 4, or TLR4, sits on the surface of immune cells. It is activated by lipopolysaccharides from the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, forming part of the mammalian innate immune response. Its cytoplasmic domain, inside the cell, passes the signal onward.

Their title states that a dimer, two copies joined, of that domain provides a specific scaffold for recruiting signalling adaptor proteins. Shape explains specificity: only the paired platform fits the right adaptors. That geometry guides drug ideas for sepsis and inflammation.
plos-pone-0000888:
Yamina Seamari, Jose Narvaez, Francisco Vico and colleagues built methods to separate two states of brain cortex activity, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cortex networks fall into a slow rhythm during deep sleep and anesthesia. Cells swing between up states, active and charged, and down states, quiet and resting, less than once a second.

Telling those states apart in recordings sounds simple but is easy to get wrong. The authors offer robust ways to do it both live, as data comes in, and later, offline. Clean state labels underpin many studies of sleep and memory. Their methods give other labs a firmer base for that work.
plos-pone-0000988:
Insuk Lee, Zhihua Li and Edward Marcotte built a cleaner probabilistic gene network for baker's yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene networks merge millions of separate observations into one model of how a cell works. For yeast, such a network is a workhorse for predicting what unstudied genes do.

The catch is bias: well studied genes gather more links just because they are well studied. The authors present an improved network with that bias reduced. A fairer map gives unknown genes a better chance of being placed correctly. Yeast networks often prototype methods later used on human data, so the fix travels.
plos-pone-0001088:
Dietrich Gotzek, D. DeWayne Shoemaker and Kenneth Ross examined gene variation behind fire ant social form, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The fire ant Solenopsis invicta comes in two social forms. Some colonies have one egg laying queen; others have many. That difference reshapes colony life entirely.

A candidate gene had been implicated in regulating this social behavior. The team study molecular variation at that gene across forms. Few traits offer so direct a line from one gene region to a whole society's structure. The fire ant is also a major invasive pest, so its social genetics carry practical weight for control efforts in the southern United States.
plos-pone-0001188:
Leptospira interrogans is a corkscrew-shaped bacterium that spreads through the bloodstream and colonizes many tissues, causing leptospirosis. Brian Stevenson and colleagues examined proteins on its outer surface in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Infectious leptospires can resist killing by the complement system, part of the immune defense in blood.

The authors show that the bacterium's endostatin-like outer membrane proteins bind host fibronectin and laminin, two proteins of the tissue scaffold, plus regulators of complement. Grabbing scaffold proteins may help the bacterium attach and invade. Binding complement regulators may help it hide. Together these tricks explain part of its success as a pathogen.
plos-pone-0001288:
Animals must sense how much sugar is available and respond, and for years attention focused on glucose sensing inside cells. Emilie Stolarczyk and colleagues studied sensing outside cells instead, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They disabled GLUT2, a glucose transporter that also acts as a sugar sensor, in mice.

The authors report that loss of sugar detection by GLUT2 affects glucose homeostasis in the mice. Homeostasis is the body's balancing of blood sugar levels. Their work shows that detection at the cell surface is a real part of that balance, not a sideshow.
plos-pone-0001388:
Fredrik Vannberg and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene variant and tuberculosis. TB kills and sickens many people each year, most of all in sub Saharan Africa. A cell receptor coded by the gene CD209 can grab and take in the TB germ. Prior work had linked a variant near this gene to TB risk.

The team tested that link in their own groups of patients and controls. They asked whether the same variant raised or lowered the odds of disease. Firm checks like this sort true risk genes from false leads. The data help guide the search for host traits that shape who falls ill with TB.
plos-pone-0001488:
Yvonne Vallès, Kenneth Halanych, and Jeffrey Boore published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on mobile DNA in an animal genome. Group II introns are RNA pieces that cut themselves out of messages and can hop to new spots. They are common in germs and cell parts, but rare in animal nuclei. They are thought to be the kin of our own splicing parts.

The team found these introns in the genome of a two sided animal, a first of its kind. That find breaks the old bounds for where they can live. It hints they were once more common in animal lines. It also adds a data point to the tale of how gene splicing arose.
plos-pone-0001588:
Jeffrey Trimarchi, Michael Stadler, and Constance Cepko wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on single eye cells in mice. The retina grows from stem like cells that read cues from their world. The varied fates of those cells must in part stem from varied gene use. The team read gene use in single retinal stem cells, one by one.

Even cells of the same type and age showed wide spread in gene use. That spread may be the raw stuff from which distinct fates are picked. Single cell reads catch what pooled samples smear out. The work sets a base for how the eye builds its many cell types.
plos-pone-0001688:
Françoise Guinet, Patrick Avé, Louis Jones, and their co-authors traced the earliest events of plague infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, evolved recently from a gut pathogen, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. In doing so it gained entry through the skin and extreme virulence. Which early events make it so deadly was the question.

The authors report two faults acting together. The innate immune cells that should attack first respond poorly, and the bacteria infiltrate lymph nodes in a distinctive way. The full text gives the infection time course, the cell counts, and the node pathology. These first hours decide whether plague takes hold, so they are also where new treatments would have to act fastest.
plos-pone-0001788:
Benjamin S. C. Uzochukwu and co-authors compared how mothers in town and countryside respond to childhood fever in south east Nigeria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Childhood fevers from malaria remain a major cause of illness and death among under-five children in Nigeria. How dangerous a mother judges the fever to be shapes what care she seeks.

The team surveyed rural and urban mothers on their perceptions of severity and their patterns of health care use. The full text gives the survey results and the rural-urban contrasts. Fever care often starts at home or with drug sellers. Knowing those first steps is essential for programs trying to get sick children treated in time.
plos-pone-0001888:
Ada De Luigi and colleagues tested a family of common drugs against prion disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Prions are rogue proteins that cause fatal brain ills in animals and in people, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. In past lab work, tetracycline drugs bound to the rogue protein and made it lose its tough, hard-to-break form.

The team asked whether that effect could slow real infection, both when prions enter the body and when they are placed in the brain. Past work had shown lower prion levels and longer life in hamsters dosed with these drugs. A cheap, known drug class that buys time would be a rare gain in a field with no cure.
plos-pone-0001988:
Paul Gilbert and co-authors tested a video counselor for HIV patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cutting drug use and unsafe sex among people with HIV helps their own health and lowers the chance they pass the virus on. Guidelines tell providers to screen and counsel for these risks, yet busy clinics often skip it.

The program, called Video Doctor, gives interactive counseling by computer in the clinic. As the title states, it reduced drug and sexual risk acts among HIV-positive patients in diverse clinics. A tool that counsels without staff time could fill a gap that human clinics struggle to close.
plos-pone-0002088:
Douglas Bakkum, Zenas Chao, and Steve Potter studied slow shifts in how brain networks pass signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Precise timing of nerve spikes is essential to many brain functions. From one neuron's view, the timings of incoming spikes from its partners decide whether it fires, and when.

The team grew cortical networks in the lab. Over the long term, they tracked how activity changed both the delay of spike travel and spike size. As the title states, this long-term, activity-dependent plasticity reshapes propagation itself. Wiring that retimes its own signals adds a layer to how networks learn.
plos-pone-0002188:
Christiane Dolecek, Tran Thi Phi La, Nguyen Ngoc Rang, and co-authors compared two antibiotics for typhoid fever in Vietnam, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drug-resistant typhoid is a growing clinical problem worldwide. Older fluoroquinolone drugs such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, once first-line treatments, had begun to fail.

The team ran a randomized controlled trial in children and adults with uncomplicated typhoid. Patients received either gatifloxacin or azithromycin, and the researchers compared cure rates and safety. Head-to-head trials like this give doctors in high-burden regions evidence for which drug to reach for when the old standbys no longer work.
plos-pone-0002288:
Conrad Earnest and co-authors reported on six months of exercise training in inactive postmenopausal women. Their 2008 PLOS ONE paper covers how training changed heart rate variability. Heart rate variability, the small timing changes between beats, falls with age and low values predict higher mortality. Postmenopausal women have lower variability than younger women, and inactivity and obesity can push it lower still.

The data come from the DREW study, a controlled trial of exercise dose in this group. The team measured whether training raised variability over six months. Results from a large, careful trial help doctors prescribe exercise with clearer expectations for heart health.
plos-pone-0002388:
Attardo and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alessio Attardo, Federico Calegari, Wulf Haubensak, and others. Its subject is live Imaging at the Onset of Cortical Neurogenesis Reveals Differential Appearance. The rest of the title points to the Neuronal Phenotype in Apical versus Basal Progenitor Progeny. The neurons of the mammal brain are made by progenitor cells that divide at one of two surfaces.

Some divide at the apical surface of the ventricular zone, and others divide at its basal side. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002488:
Led by Swaddle, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from John P. Swaddle, Stavros E. Calos, and others. Its subject is increased Avian Diversity Is Associated with Lower Incidence of Human West Nile Infection: Observation of the Dilution Effect.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002588:
Research by Massacand and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Joanna C. Massacand, Patrick Kaiser, Bettina Ernst, and others. Its subject is intestinal Bacteria Condition Dendritic Cells to Promote IgA Production. Immunoglobulin (Ig) A represents the predominant antibody isotype produced at the intestinal mucosa.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002688:
Research from Abhay Kumar Thakur and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers UV-Light exposed prion protein fails to form amyloid fibrils. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Abhay Kumar Thakur, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Amyloid fibril formation involves three steps; structural perturbation, nucleation and elongation. The authors add a further point. We have investigated amyloidogenesis using prion protein as a model system and UV-light as a structural perturbant. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002788:
Work by Kamaldeen Baba and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was adenosine deaminase activity is a sensitive marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis in patients with very low CD4 counts. The catalog record names Kamaldeen Baba first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Adenosine Deaminase Activity (ADA) is a commonly used marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleural effusion. The authors add a further point. There has been concern about its usefulness in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV positive patients with very low CD4 counts. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002888:
Anne-Pierre Morel, Marjory Lièvre, Clémence Thomas and colleagues linked two big cancer ideas in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One idea holds that cancer stem cells start tumors. The other holds that epithelial cells spread by first changing form, a shift called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or EMT.

Working with a mammary tumor model, the team reports that forcing that shift can generate breast cancer stem cells. The title states that result directly. If the two processes are joined, a drug that blocks the shift might also curb the stem cells that regrow tumors after treatment.
plos-pone-0002988:
Naomi Willis, Thomas Cox, Syed Rahman-Casañs and co-authors named lamin A/C a risk marker in colorectal cancer in 2008. A-type lamins are structural proteins of the cell nucleus, coded by the LMNA gene. Faults in that gene cause several early-ageing and degenerative diseases.

Lamins also affect the retinoblastoma protein and cancer genes such as beta-catenin, both relevant to bowel cancer. The PLOS ONE study evaluates lamin A/C as a biomarker, a measurable sign of risk or outlook. A reliable marker could help sort patients by likely course and treatment need. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003088:
Marcel Kool, Jan Koster, Jens Bunt and co-authors split medulloblastoma into five subtypes by integrated genomics in 2008. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Cure rates had improved, but predicting outcome was still a major challenge and survivors suffer serious therapy side effects.

Combining genetics, pathway signatures, and clinical features yielded five subtypes with distinct profiles, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, finer subtypes let doctors spare low-risk children the harshest treatment. The classification also gives drug research defined targets instead of one mixed disease. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003188:
Alice Hadchouel, Fabrice Decobert, Marie-Laure Franco-Montoya and colleagues link gene variants to a preterm lung disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Building the air sacs of the lung requires coordinated remodeling of the matrix outside cells, in which matrix metalloproteinases, or MMPs, play an important role. The team postulated that variants in MMP genes might affect MMP function in preterm lungs and alter the risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Their title reports identification of MMP16 as a new player in lung development. Readers see a candidate gene for a serious disease of premature infants. Genetic risk clues may one day help target closer monitoring.
plos-pone-0003288:
Ming Yi and Robert M. Stephens present a pathway ranking method in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Analysis of microarray and other high throughput data often involves identification of genes consistently up or down-regulated across samples as the first step in extraction of biological meaning. This gene-level paradigm can be limited as a result of valid sample fluctuations and noise.

Their method, SLEPR, is a sample-level enrichment-based pathway ranking approach seeking biological themes through pathway-level consistency. Readers get a shift from single gene lists to whole pathway patterns. Pathway views often survive noise better and point more directly to disease processes.
plos-pone-0007388: An HIV vaccine must outsmart a virus that mutates constantly, and this study argues the key is choosing the right vaccine sequences. It proposes candidate protein sequences built to cover the variation of HIV-1 both within a single strain family and across different ones. The goal is to train the immune system's killer T cells to hit targets the virus cannot easily change.
plos-pone-0007488: When DNA suffers double-strand breaks, cells repair them — but sloppy repairs can fuse the wrong chromosomes, a hallmark of cancer. Using baker's yeast, this study shows a repair protein called Msh2 blocks a backup repair route that would otherwise trim broken ends incorrectly. The finding reveals a safeguard that keeps chromosome fusions from forming after damage.
plos-pone-0007588: After a stopped heart is restarted, the heart muscle itself often falters. This study tested mild cooling plus a protective drug treatment in resuscitated animals and found the combination reduced heart dysfunction. It worked by calming inflammation, limiting cell death, and slowing harmful remodeling — extending the known benefits of cooling beyond the brain.
plos-pone-0007688: Zebrafish aging got a telomere check. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Lund's team found telomerase and telomere length ignore age and fin regrowth in zebrafish. The ageless-telomere result was logged. The check feeds aging science.
